title: "Exploratory Data Analysis"
format: typst
---

```{r setup}
library(tidyverse)

# read precinct-level statement-of-vote data
g24_prec <- readr::read_csv("data/g24_sov_by_g24_svprec.csv")

# keep and clean the congressional vote columns
g24_cng <- g24_prec |>
  mutate(
    CNGDEM01 = as.numeric(CNGDEM01),
    CNGREP01 = as.numeric(CNGREP01),
    CNGIND01 = as.numeric(CNGIND01)
  )

# build a district-level summary we can reuse for all questions
district_results <- g24_cng |>
  filter(CDDIST != 0) |>             # drop statewide total row (CDDIST == 0)
  group_by(CDDIST) |>
  summarise(
    dem_votes = sum(CNGDEM01, na.rm = TRUE),
    rep_votes = sum(CNGREP01, na.rm = TRUE),
    ind_votes = sum(CNGIND01, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    total_votes = dem_votes + rep_votes + ind_votes,
    dem_share = dem_votes / (dem_votes + rep_votes),
    rep_share = rep_votes / (dem_votes + rep_votes),
    winner_party = if_else(dem_share > rep_share, "DEM", "REP"),
    margin = abs(dem_share - rep_share)
  )


```


Question 1

How many congressional seats did each party win in 2024, and how does that compare to their statewide share of the two-party vote?

number of seats by party

seat_counts <- district_results |>
count(winner_party, name = "n_seats")

seat_counts

statewide vote totals and shares (two-party only)

statewide_totals <- district_results |>
summarise(
dem_votes = sum(dem_votes),
rep_votes = sum(rep_votes)
) |>
mutate(
dem_share_statewide = dem_votes / (dem_votes + rep_votes),
rep_share_statewide = rep_votes / (dem_votes + rep_votes)
)

statewide_totals

Answer 1

Using the district-level summaries, Democrats win 43 of the 52 congressional seats (about 82.7%), while Republicans win 9 seats (about 17.3%).

Statewide, however, Democrats receive about 60.7% of the two-party vote for Congress, and Republicans receive about 39.3%.
So Democrats win a noticeably larger share of seats than their share of the vote, while Republicans win fewer seats than their vote share would suggest.

Question 2

Which districts had the closest races in 2024, and what were the winning margins?


closest_races <- district_results |>
arrange(margin) |>
mutate(margin_pct = 100 * margin) |>
slice_head(n = 5)

closest_races

Answer 2

Looking at the difference in two-party vote share between the winner and the runner-up:

District 45 is the closest race:
the Democrat receives 158,216 votes and the Republican 157,522 votes, a margin of only about 0.2 percentage points.

Other very close races include

District 27 (margin ≈ 2.7 percentage points),

District 47 (margin ≈ 2.9 points),

District 13 (margin ≈ 3.1 points), and

District 41 (margin ≈ 3.3 points, won by the Republican).

These districts would be the most competitive under the 2024 map.

Question 3

How are Democratic vote shares across districts distributed? Are most districts competitive, or are many seats “safe” for one party?

library(ggplot2)

summary stats for Democratic share across districts

summary(district_results$dem_share)

histogram of dem_share

ggplot(district_results, aes(x = dem_share)) +
geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.05) +
scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
labs(
x = "Democratic two-party vote share",
y = "Number of districts",
title = "Distribution of Democratic vote share across districts (2024)"
)

Answer 3

Across districts, the Democratic two-party vote share has:

a median around 63%,

an interquartile range from roughly 52% to 69%, and

extremes ranging from 0% (solid Republican districts) to 100% (uncontested Democratic districts).

The histogram shows that many districts are not very competitive: a large share of districts are strongly Democratic, a smaller group are strongly Republican, and only a handful fall near the 50–50 range. This pattern suggests a map with many “safe” seats and relatively few true swing districts.
